newsitem.title: FINLAND: Clinton, Yeltsin end summit, U.S. hails progress.
newsitem.headline: Clinton, Yeltsin end summit, U.S. hails progress.

text.p: U.S. President Bill Clinton and Russian President Boris Yeltsin ended their summit on Friday and American officials hailed it as a success, although the two leaders "agreed to disagree" on NATO expansion.
The two sides were expected to issue joint statements, including one each on European security and economic issues, as the leaders prepared for a news conference at 1645 GMT.

A senior U.S. official told Reuters they had made "progress on all fronts" although he said they had been unable to bridge the gulf over NATO enlargement, the biggest problem dividing Russia and the West in the post-Cold War era.
But this had not apparently caused a rift. Clinton and Yeltsin had decided to stick to the path of cooperation and "agreed to disagree" on NATO expansion, the official said.
There was significant progress on arms control, the official said, with the prospect of fresh U.S.-Russian talks on deeper cuts in long-range nuclear weapons.
The two men also discussed a comprehensive plan to boost U.S. investment in Russia's fledgling market economy and Moscow pressed Washington for membership of the developed world's economic clubs.
No immediate comment was available from the Russian side.
Friday's talks, held at the official residence of Finnish President Martti Ahtisaari overlooking a partly-frozen Baltic Sea, lasted a total of just over four hours.
Both Clinton and Yeltsin have said they were willing to seek compromises in difficult areas and seemed determined to confound predictions that the summit would fail on differences over NATO.

Moscow bitterly opposes NATO's plans to take in former Soviet-bloc states in Eastern Europe, saying it would isolate and threaten Russia. Washington says NATO will take in new members as planned and that all Europe will benefit as a result.
A NATO summit in July is expected to invite Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic to start accession talks. The new members would not join until 1999 at the earliest.

Earlier, spokesmen for both sides described the initial two-hour session of talks as intense but not argumentative. Russian officials said there was progress on how to build better links between the 16-nation alliance and Moscow.
White House spokesman Mike McCurry said the opening session on Friday was "substantive and intense".

Yeltsin, under strong pressure from communist and nationalist critics at home who accuse him of selling out to the West, said earlier on Friday that he had not been convinced by Western arguments on NATO expansion.

But there was some progress, according to the Kremlin, on NATO's offer to forge a new, formal relationship with Russia that would give Moscow more of a say in European security without allowing it to veto alliance decisions.
Although Russia opposes NATO enlargement, it does want closer ties with its old Cold War foe and has been negotiating the terms of the relationship with the alliance.

Despite some thundering rhetoric from the Kremlin and displays of steely resolve from Washington in advance of the summit, the two leaders seemed upbeat before Friday's session, relying on their good personal relationship to see them through.

The two men are meeting for the 11th time, although they have not seen each other for almost a year. Clinton is confined to a wheelchair following a leg injury, while Yeltsin is still recovering from heart surgery and months of illness.
To make sure Yeltsin stands firm on NATO, his domestic opponents in the Russian parliament (Duma) planned a strident anti-Western debate on NATO for Friday.
Russian Communist Party leader Gennady Zyuganov blasted Yeltsin's foreign policy before the debate, saying the president was incapable of defending Moscow's interests at the summit.
Clinton, too, is under pressure over NATO enlargement.

Eastern European nations, including the Baltic republics that lie just across the water from Helsinki, are watching closely to see there are no secret deals cut with Moscow over the future of Europe -- as in 1945, at the end of World War Two.
The U.S. president returns to Washington later on Friday, while Yeltsin was scheduled to stay on for talks with Ahtisaari on Saturday before flying back to Moscow.
